newsitem.title: MALDIVES: Pakistan vows to address all issues with India.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan vows to address all issues with India.

text.p: Pakistan Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif on Monday promised to try to resolve all disputes with India as the longtime rivals prepared to hold their highest-level talks in four years.

Sharif was scheduled to meet Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral after the inauguration of a South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) summit in the capital of the Maldives islands in the Indian Ocean.

It would be the first face-to-face meeting between the leaders of the two South Asian neighbours since April 1993, when Sharif and then Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao met on the sidelines of a SAARC conference.
It would follow two rounds of talks between lower-level officials in March and April this year.
"We are determined to continue with this progress so that all outstanding issues can be comprehensively addressed," Sharif said in a speech prepared for delivery at the SAARC inaugural ceremony.

"With sincerity and resolve we can overcome these problems and establish good neighbourly and cooperative relations. The dividends of success will be enormous, not only for Pakistan and India, but also for the entire SAARC region."
Sharif took office once more in February after general elections, while Gujral was named prime minister on April 19 following a three-week political crisis in India.
They exchanged letters shortly after Gujral took power, expressing a common desire to press ahead with the peace talks that followed three years of recrimination over the divided region of Kashmir.
Both Sharif and Gujral arrived in the Maldives, a windswept archipelago located 500 km (300 miles) southwest of the southern tip of India, on Sunday.

They were to join leaders from Bangladesh, Bhutan, the Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka at the opening of the three-day SAARC summit on Monday before holding about two hours of face-to-face talks in the afternoon, Indian officials said.
The two leaders were expected to hold a joint news conference at about 3:30 p.m. (1000 GMT).
Diplomats described the informal meeting as an ice-breaking session, and played down expectations that any major announcements would be made.

But the two prime ministers were expected to instruct their foreign secretaries -- the highest ranking civil servants in their foreign ministries -- to a second round of talks in late May or early June in Islamabad.
The first round was held in New Delhi in late March, followed by a meeting of the two foreign ministers in April.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since they were carved out of British India in 1947, two of them over the Himalayan region of Kashmir.
Police and hospital officials say more than 20,000 people have died in a separatist revolt in India's Jammu and Kashmir state since the conflict erupted in 1990.

Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan said on Sunday that a settlement over Kashmir would take "a long time", but progress in other areas such as relaxing travel restrictions, boosting trade and releasing prisoners could be expected sooner.
India, which would prefer to address less contentious issues before Kashmir, welcomed Khan's comments.

"That makes sense to us because that is what we have been saying, that intractable issues cannot be settled overnight," Indian Foreign Ministry spokesman Talmiz Ahmad told Reuters Television, citing Kashmir.
